1817年由巴黎製樂器師Jean Hilaire Asté發明，用以延伸鍵號低音: It was invented in 1817 by the Parisian instrument maker Jean Hilaire Asté to extend the low range of the keyed bugle and to replace the serpent. The 1821 patent lists bass, alto and contrabass models; the stage band of the opera Olimpie used one as early as 1819. The bass model took root in nineteenth-century West European military bands and in the brass section of the orchestra, then, with the rise of valve instruments, was replaced at the end of the nineteenth century by the euphonium and the early tuba; it also entered Brazilian choro bands and stayed there into the twentieth century, and was revived at the end of the twentieth century through historically informed performance.

奧菲克萊德號主要由黃銅製成，管身採用錐形黃銅管材，具有良好的共鳴特性。活塞按鍵系: The ophicleide is mostly made of brass, its body of tapered brass tubing, which resonates well. The key mechanism is of nickel silver or cupronickel, for durability and precise action. The mouthpiece is of brass or silver and is smaller than a tuba's. The inside of the body may be nickel- or silver-plated to prevent oxidation. On some finer instruments the key tubing is stainless steel or another alloy, to improve the tone and lengthen the instrument's life.
奧菲克萊德號屬鍵式銅管，初學先以杯狀吹嘴與口風取得泛音，再依按鍵開閉音孔改變氣柱: The ophicleide is a keyed brass instrument: a beginner first finds the harmonics with a cup mouthpiece and the embouchure, then opens and closes the tone holes with the keys to change the length of the air column. Most of its tone holes are normally closed and open only when a key is pressed; the largest hole below the bell is normally open and closes when pressed, which lengthens the air column and lowers the pitch by a semitone. The left hand controls three normally closed holes and the normally open top hole; in the middle and upper range the left hand alone can play, while the right hand holds the instrument steady. The lowest range needs the right hand on the smaller holes near the mouthpiece, and alternative fingerings can be used to improve intonation.
奧菲克萊德號曾見於十九世紀歐洲軍樂隊、管弦樂團低音銅管、歌劇與英國、法國市民銅管: The ophicleide appeared in nineteenth-century European military bands, in the low brass of orchestras, in opera and in British and French civic brass bands, and it was also used in Brazilian choro bands. Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique and his Requiem, among other works, call for it; today it appears in historically informed performances and in ensembles in London and Sydney.
奧菲克萊德號為19世紀法國發明的按鍵銅管氣鳴樂器，H-S分類423.21。管身呈: The ophicleide is a keyed brass aerophone invented in France in the nineteenth century, H-S 423.21. Its body is conical, its length and folding close to those of an upright serpent, the bell flares only slightly, and it takes a cup mouthpiece. It is played by opening and closing tone holes with keys: the left hand controls the main holes, and the right hand works the smaller holes in the low range. It was used in military bands, civic brass bands and the low brass of early Romantic orchestras, and in Brazilian choro bands, and was later replaced by the euphonium, the tuba and the like.
奧菲克萊德號音色深沉厚重，具有獨特的木質感與金屬光澤並存的特性。其低音域寬廣而富: The ophicleide's timbre is deep and heavy, with the unusual quality of woodenness and metallic sheen at once. Its low range is broad and penetrating, and its tone lies between the warmth of the horn and the roughness of the tuba, with the brass character clearly present. The instrument uses a key mechanism, so intonation is fairly stable and the resonance full and ample. Beside the vague, murky serpent the ophicleide is clearer and stronger; beside the modern tuba its tone is a little gentler, lacking the tuba's direct attack but with a classical grace of its own. In a band its timbre can lay a solid bass foundation and, in solo, show an expressive character full of personality.
